name: Cache-line padding of per-thread partial sums (false-sharing avoidance)
listed_description: Per-thread accumulators are spaced at least 64 bytes apart, or kept in thread-local variables, so threads stop fighting over one cache line; the book also points to the C++17 hardware_destructive_interference_size constant.
claim_text: Without false sharing the sum accumulation stays approximately twice as fast (Figure 5.8), and scales perfectly with threads.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, multi-threaded sum accumulation of unsigned long increments into an adjacent per-thread array versus padded or local partial sums, 1 to 16+ threads on an x86 server; compiler, flags and exact CPU not stated in the text. Code in companion Chapter05.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 5, section 'Why data sharing is expensive'

name: std::atomic counter increment versus mutex-guarded counter
listed_description: Replace a std::mutex plus lock_guard around a shared counter with an atomic fetch_add; the book measures both on one to many threads.
claim_text: Single-thread mutex-guarded increment costs 23 nanoseconds versus 7 nanoseconds for the atomic increment; the gap widens with threads.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, shared counter increment from 1 to 16 threads, std::atomic versus std::mutex with lock_guard; compiler, flags and CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter05 and Chapter06.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 5, section 'Understanding the cost of memory synchronization'; ch. 6, section 'Locks, alternatives, and their performance'

name: Optimized spinlock (test-and-test-and-set with bounded spin then 1 ns nanosleep)
listed_description: Spinlock whose waiters read the flag with relaxed loads and only attempt an exchange when it looks free, sleeping about 1 ns after 8 failed attempts; compared with std::mutex, a CAS loop and an atomic add for a shared counter.
claim_text: The spinlock soundly outperforms the compare-and-swap implementation and gives the wait-free atomic operation tough competition (Figure 6.2); naive version terrible.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, shared counter increment on 1 to many threads on two x86 systems (Figure 6.3), mutex versus spinlock versus CAS versus atomic add; numbers only in figures; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter06 (01c_spinlock_count.C).
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 6, section 'Different locks for different problems'

name: Pointer spinlock (lock that owns the guarded object pointer)
listed_description: Spinlock variant where the atomic holds a pointer to the guarded object and lock() returns it, so unlocked access is impossible.
claim_text: This lock slightly outperforms the regular spinlock more often than not (Figure 6.3); result varies by processor.
book_benchmark: Same shared-counter Google Benchmark as the spinlock entry, two x86 systems, 1 to many threads; numbers only in figures; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter06 (01d_ptrlock_count.C).
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 6, section 'Counters and accumulators'

name: Publishing pointer (ts_unique_ptr, release/acquire atomic root pointer)
listed_description: Owning pointer whose publish() stores with release order and get() loads with acquire order, giving lock-free one-producer publication of immutable data to many readers.
claim_text: Single-threaded dereference matches a raw pointer and std::unique_ptr; the publishing pointer is 60 times faster than an atomic std::shared_ptr on one thread.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of pointer dereference by 1 to many consumer threads: publishing pointer versus raw pointer versus std::shared_ptr with atomic_load_explicit (Figures 6.5 to 6.7); compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter06 (03_owning_ptr_mbm.C).
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 6, section 'Smart pointers for concurrent programming', Publishing pointer

name: Minimal intrusive atomic shared pointer (no weak pointer, count in object)
listed_description: Custom reference-counted pointer storing the count inside the pointee and dropping std::shared_ptr features such as weak pointers and control block, with atomic publish and load.
claim_text: A minimalistic reference-counted pointer can be several times more efficient than the standard one (Figure 6.8); still much slower than a unique pointer.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of concurrent consumer-thread loads and assignment through the atomic shared publishing pointer, custom versus std::shared_ptr atomic access; numbers only in figures; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter06 (04_intr_shared_ptr_mbm.C and atomic shared pointer sample).
guessed_baseline: std::shared_ptr with atomic access functions, C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 6, section 'Smart pointers for concurrent programming', Atomic shared pointer

name: Batched push/pop on a mutex-guarded stack (1,024 elements per lock)
listed_description: Thread-safe stack API that moves many elements per lock acquisition, plus an unlocked single-threaded bulk push for upfront loading.
claim_text: Pushing 1,024 elements under one lock/unlock is faster than locking per element (Figure 7.5); locked stack single-thread is over 10x slower than plain std::stack.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of a std::stack wrapper (mt_stack) guarded by std::mutex, push/pop item pairs, 1 to 8 threads, batch versus single; about 30M ops/s on one thread and 3.1M on 8 versus about 485M for unlocked std::stack on the same x86 machine; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter07 (02_stack.C).
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, sections 'Performance of mutex-guarded data structures' and 'Performance requirements for different uses'

name: Spinlock-guarded thread-safe stack and queue
listed_description: Thread-safe std::stack and std::queue wrappers guarded by the book's spinlock instead of std::mutex, shown as hard to beat with a lock-free design on x86.
claim_text: Spinlock stack about 70M operations per second on the x86 machine versus 30M for the mutex stack on one thread (Figures 7.3, 7.11).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, push-then-pop item pairs, 1 to 8+ threads, x86 and a large ARM server; spinlock versus std::mutex versus unlocked std::stack/std::queue (about 280M items/s unlocked queue); compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter07.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, sections 'Stack performance in detail' and 'The thread-safe queue'

name: Lock-free array stack (packed producer and consumer indices, CAS, yield on contention)
listed_description: Fixed-capacity stack using two indices in one 64-bit atomic word updated with compare-and-swap, with nanosleep or yield after a few failed CAS tries.
claim_text: On x86 it does not outperform the spinlock version; on ARM the lock-free stack is much faster at large thread counts (Figure 7.16).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, push/pop pairs on x86 and a large ARM HPC server, 1 to many threads, lock-free versus spinlock-guarded versus mutex-guarded stack; numbers only in figures except the spinlock x86 reference of about 70M ops/s; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter07.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, section 'Lock-free stack'

name: Lock-free single-producer single-consumer circular-buffer queue
listed_description: Fixed-size circular buffer queue with separate atomic head and tail indices for exactly one producer thread and one consumer thread.
claim_text: About 100M integers per second on x86, same as the lock-guarded queue; clearly better on ARM and for large (copy-heavy) elements (Figures 7.20, 7.21).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, one producer and one consumer thread, queue of integers and of large structs, lock-based versus lock-free, x86 and ARM; compiler, flags, CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter07.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, section 'Lock-free queue'

name: Non-sequentially-consistent queue (array of single-threaded sub-queues owned via atomic pointer exchange)
listed_description: Relaxed-ordering concurrent queue made of several single-threaded sub-queues; a thread takes exclusive ownership of one by atomically swapping its pointer with null.
claim_text: With 1 KB elements, spinlock std::queue gets about 170k elements/s on one thread and drops to 130k on many; this queue scales (Figure 7.23).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark on a large x86 server, all threads doing push and pop of 1 KB elements, many threads, versus spinlock-guarded std::queue; compiler, flags and CPU not stated. Code in companion Chapter07.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, section 'Non-sequentially consistent data structures'

name: Lock-free singly-linked list with shared_ptr nodes and iterators
listed_description: Concurrent forward list using smart pointers for nodes and iterators, with CAS at the head and the ABA problem and reclamation discussed (hazard pointers, RCU mentioned).
claim_text: Spinlock list is faster for head insert/delete; for long-list traversals concurrent with insertions the lock-free list is faster by as much as you want.
book_benchmark: Qualitative comparison of spinlock-guarded versus lock-free singly linked list, push_front/pop_front and traversal under concurrent insertion; no numbers in text. Code in companion Chapter07.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 7, section 'Lock-free list'

name: C++17 parallel STL algorithms (std::execution::par for std::sort and std::for_each)
listed_description: Parallel execution policies on standard algorithms, run in GCC and Clang through the Intel TBB runtime, benchmarked against sequential execution at several sizes.
claim_text: Parallel std::sort shows very good speedup on large inputs, but is slower than sequential at 1024 elements because threads start per call.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, std::for_each with expensive work(), cheap increment, and std::sort on vector<double>, 2 threads, sequential versus par policy, sizes 1024 to 32K and larger; GCC or Clang with TBB, flags and CPU not stated; numbers only in figures 8.1 to 8.4. Code in companion Chapter08 (parallel_algorithm.C).
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 8, section 'Concurrency support in C++17'

name: oneTBB (Intel Threading Building Blocks)
listed_description: Threading library that provides the runtime under GCC and Clang parallel STL; each compiler version needs the matching TBB version.
claim_text: Book credits no TBB-specific numbers; its parallel std::sort and std::for_each results (ch. 8 figures) ran on this runtime.
book_benchmark: Indirect: parallel algorithm benchmarks in Chapter08 use TBB as backend; poor speed on short sequences blamed on thread start per algorithm call in the GCC/Clang integration.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 8, section 'Concurrency support in C++17'
